title: Observation when functional limitation does not track the hernia
fairness: The best offered plan is observation with return precautions. The resident must separate the running-related adduction pain from the painless protrusion during usual warehouse lifting, then apply the selected-male observation boundary and the patient's preference.

The preference to defer is necessary decision context, not an unfair instruction to choose observation: it would not justify observing a hernia with a different risk profile or attributable functional limitation. Elective repair remains discussable, but arranging it now is less aligned with this particular record. Repeating ultrasound is the weaker distractor because a dynamic sac and reduction are already established.

The task is complete and the node stands alone. No confident clinical inaccuracy identified. This report reviews only current candidate display text, not author gates or earlier verdicts; no network or independent source verification was performed. PASS is an editorial judgment, not Melissa Rowland's clinical approval, and difficulty predictions are qualitative.

title: Threatened partial bowel wall despite continued stool passage
fairness: Emergency operative exploration is the single best offered intervention. The partial-circumference anatomy explains why stool passage is not reassuring; substantially reduced enhancement and fixed tenderness then make a reduction attempt inappropriate. These are observations requiring clinical interpretation, not a pre-answer diagnosis of strangulation.

Manual reduction is a credible consequential error if the learner overweights ongoing stool passage. Elective discharge planning is a weaker distractor. The explanation appropriately distinguishes suspected ischemia from proven irreversible necrosis.

The hospital chart-review frame and hospital-directed task agree, with initial support already underway. The current record supplies the needed context independently of any later bowel-resection item. No confident clinical inaccuracy identified.

title: Repair of recurrence after an open posterior mesh operation
clarityIssues: The standalone update begins 'At a later clinic review' and refers to 'the site of the lifting episode', although no lifting episode or earlier review is supplied in the presentation. The presentation only says 'a new symptom'. These are unresolved references left from a sequence.

The task calls the recurrence symptomatic, but the displayed clinical history does not identify the symptom or its relationship to the recurrent protrusion. A reader should not have to infer a missing earlier case part.
fairness: Conditional on the stated symptomatic recurrence, open anterior Lichtenstein repair is the best offered answer. Interpreting the mesh position rather than the skin incision identifies the previously used posterior plane; that finding changes the preferred recurrence approach.

TAPP and TEP are credible errors for a learner who mistakes every open operation for an anterior repair. Their shared posterior compartment is clinically meaningful rather than a nonmedical convergence shortcut. No confident clinical inaccuracy identified in the repair principle.
The clinical decision is salvageable with a small standalone-context repair. An earlier PASS designation does not resolve the missing referent in the candidate display reviewed here.
suggestions: Replace the opening temporal reference with a current clinic presentation and state the actual lifting-associated symptom and recurrent contour in one short sentence. Remove 'later' and 'the lifting episode' unless the relevant earlier events are explicitly supplied.
Preserve the operative-plane observations and the three competing repairs; the difficulty should continue to come from interpreting an open posterior operation, not reconstructing missing chronology.

title: Small directly closable groin defect after gross enteric spillage
fairness: Primary tissue closure is the best offered repair for this small, directly closable defect after perforation and gross enteric contamination. The resident must distinguish this field from controlled bowel entry and then use defect size and closure feasibility to distinguish tissue closure from biologic reinforcement.

'Approximate its edges without tension' is necessary information for that comparison, not an expendable permission sentence. Removing it would weaken the ranking against biologic reconstruction. The options name actual repairs with comparable specificity.

The explanation limits the recommendation to this setting and explicitly acknowledges older, low-certainty guidance. The precise guideline boundary quoted in the explanation was not independently source-verified in this offline review; no confident clinical inaccuracy is asserted. The hospital operative-record task stands alone.

title: Elective repair of an asymptomatic marked femoral swelling
fairness: Elective groin repair is the single best offered plan. The marker identifies which of two abnormalities is being asked about. The resident must localize that sac to the femoral compartment and then reject extrapolating the minimally symptomatic male inguinal observation policy to it.

The painless, reducing examination and preference for deferral make surveillance a credible competing choice. The lack of an acute painful irreducible presentation distinguishes elective repair from emergency exploration. The marked versus cranial labels identify targets without naming the diagnosis or keyed plan.

The exhibit is explicitly constructed, internally understandable and necessary to the decision: deleting it removes the anatomy that defeats observation. The named patient, age, sex and complete task are present. No prior case part is required and no confident clinical inaccuracy identified.

title: Persistent deep scrotal pain after a cutaneous block response
clarityIssues: 'Before the specialist's injection, touching the area was too painful to distinguish the two' does not identify what examination was limited or how touching was intended to distinguish a clothing-triggered symptom from a lifting-triggered symptom.

The long sequence of injection, pinprick change, clothing response, deep compression and anesthetic washout makes a straightforward referral-target question harder to read without creating a corresponding decision tradeoff.

cues.phrase: 'compression of the palpable right testicular body still reproduces the lifting ache' / 'Urological assessment of the scrotal contents'
cues.why: The explicit organ localization closely names the only organ-focused referral. Ordinary organ-to-specialty matching can select it without interpreting the block, its sensory distribution or the return of burning. The finding is clinically relevant, but it supplies a shortcut through the purported two-step task.

cues.phrase: 'Through that skin' / 'the superficial burning returns while the deeper ache persists'
cues.why: Repeated surface-versus-content framing rehearses the distinction embodied by the only contents-focused option. Repetition strengthens the shortcut rather than requiring a new interpretation.

fairness: Urological assessment is reasonable for a persistent ache reproduced at the testicular body, and the explanation appropriately does not claim a proven testicular diagnosis or exclude every neural contribution. No confident clinical inaccuracy identified.

Deleting the block details still leaves a testicle-provoked symptom and the same organ-focused referral as the best offered answer. Thus the block interpretation is not a consequential prerequisite to the scored action.

A cutaneous response does not independently exclude genital-branch pain or structural recurrence. The displayed history contains little actual recurrence assessment, so the relative priority of those alternatives deserves clinician confirmation rather than treating the block as their exclusion. This is a limitation of the ranking, not a claim that either alternative is definitely equally correct.

The node stands alone chronologically. Distinguishing postrepair neuropathic pain from scrotal-content symptoms is worthwhile resident content, but this version mainly tests a direct localization-to-referral association.
suggestions: Clarify the examination that was previously limited and shorten repeated descriptions of the same superficial response.

Redesign the comparison so a component-specific response changes the actual next action between credible competitors. Check that changing or removing the response changes the answer; merely retaining an explicit testicular tenderness-to-urology mapping will not accomplish this.

Provide any decision-critical recurrence examination or sensory findings needed to rank the referrals, with clinical support. Do not invent a rule that a successful skin block excludes recurrence or all neural causes. If a supported consequential comparison cannot be built, seek explicit acceptance as a basic localization item or park it.

title: Targeted dynamic imaging after an examination of a different site
fairness: Dynamic groin ultrasound is the best offered next investigation. The learner must establish from the acquisition record, reproduced symptom and video location that the prior study did not test the new contour, then distinguish an initial appropriately targeted study from escalation after an adequate negative study.

Dynamic MRI is a credible alternative for unresolved groin uncertainty after appropriate initial assessment. The signed worksheet and matching cine loops matter: the packet describes what was acquired rather than assuming an acquisition was omitted because exported images are missing. CT is less competitive for this intermittent, reducing contour but remains a real investigation in the same option category.

The word 'sonographer' is not an unfair instruction to repeat ultrasound: the necessary inference is whether the previous acquisition assessed the same site and provoking condition. The task is complete, the chronology is locally supplied, and no earlier node is needed. No confident clinical inaccuracy identified.

title: Posterior repair after recurrence of an anterior mesh repair
fairness: TEP is the single best offered operation. The cord, inguinal-floor mesh and external-oblique relationships establish prior anterior repair; the resident must then apply the recurrence-plane principle to the named procedures.

Lichtenstein repeats the prior compartment, and Shouldice changes the material strategy without escaping that compartment. These represent distinct credible errors. The cholecystectomy history can test overgeneralization from abdominal surgery to relevant pelvic dissection without falsely describing a scarred preperitoneal pelvis.

The explanation appropriately avoids claiming superiority of TEP over an unoffered TAPP. The symptom-related functional limitation, current recurrence, operative history and available techniques are supplied within this node. No confident clinical inaccuracy or standalone-context gap identified.

title: Initial management of a recently irreducible inguinal hernia
fairness: A gentle manual reduction attempt is the best offered initial plan in the stated hospital surgical setting. The resident must recognize acute irreducibility and then use trajectory, skin, abdominal and systemic findings to distinguish it from a presentation that raises sufficient concern for strangulation to favor immediate exploration.

Exploration represents equating every acute irreducibility with suspected ischemia; CT represents routinely requiring imaging despite an established inguinal episode and a reassuring clinical course. Both are credible nearby decisions. The necessary negative findings do not literally announce the answer or constitute gratuitous exclusions.

The clock times describe onset and reassessment, not a universal safe reduction window. The explanation retains failed reduction and emerging ischemic concern as escalation triggers and does not claim viability is guaranteed. No confident clinical inaccuracy identified; assessment for ischemia remains a clinical judgment, not a negative-examination proof.
The hospital setting, initial decision and current findings are all supplied locally, so the node stands alone.

title: Wound classification and mesh consideration after controlled resection
clarityIssues: 'Permanent mesh is eligible now' sounds like a categorical eligibility rule and leaves the mesh type unspecified. Only the post-answer explanation narrows this to macroporous permanent synthetic mesh and acknowledges weak evidence.
The lead-in requests two scored labels, field classification and material eligibility. Their relationship does not produce a changed action among the two field classes actually offered.
fairness: The intended clean-contaminated classification with consideration of macroporous permanent synthetic mesh is defensible for controlled resection without gross spillage, perforation, pus or peritonitis. No confident clinical inaccuracy is asserted, and the explanation appropriately stops short of mandating mesh over all tissue repairs.

The wording before the answer does not carry the material qualification on which the explanation relies. Broad 'permanent mesh' eligibility should not be taught as interchangeable with consideration of the particular mesh described afterward.

The four combinations are balanced, so there is no simple majority-component convergence cue. However, both clean and clean-contaminated fields permit consideration of mesh in this comparison. Correctly classifying the field therefore does not consequentially change the action; the learner answers two separable classification/eligibility checks. The clean-field/ineligible option is especially weak because no independent reason for ineligibility is supplied.
The operative record stands alone and adequately supplies the contamination facts. The deficiency is the scored comparison and material precision, not missing earlier case history.
suggestions: Specify the relevant macroporous permanent synthetic material before the choice, and describe it as an option that can be considered rather than an unqualified universal eligibility designation.

Rebuild one focused management comparison in which interpreting the contamination record actually changes the permissible or preferred plan. Use credible contamination-related mistakes and preserve the distinction between allowing mesh and establishing its superiority to tissue repair.

If retaining a classification-plus-plan matrix, make the classification consequential to the plan and recheck component balance. Do not add a second label solely to claim two-step difficulty or invent a stronger repair recommendation than the clinical evidence supports.

title: Repair and anesthesia planning after retropubic prostate surgery
fairness: Lichtenstein repair with local infiltration is a defensible favored plan among the three choices. The resident must recognize the prior pelvic/retropubic dissection from the operative description, apply it to approach selection, and distinguish local from general anesthesia for an experienced team's cooperative patient with a reducing open-repair target.

The patient is not presented as unable to tolerate general anesthesia, and the explanation correctly does not make prior prostate surgery an absolute prohibition on expert laparoscopy. The wording 'should be favored' allows a preferred plan without pretending the other techniques are universally contraindicated.

Cooperation during supine examination and experience with the offered combinations are legitimate conditions for the anesthesia comparison. They are not unique availability permissions, and the fit patient's activity makes TEP/general anesthesia a credible competing default. The key is not the most frequent combination of components: both open repair and general anesthesia appear twice.

The precise strength of the approach and anesthesia preferences has not been independently source-verified here and still requires clinician sign-off. No confident clinical inaccuracy identified from the candidate text. The operative history and current hernia state are supplied within this standalone node.
